newsitem.title: TURKEY: Army has final say in democracy Turkish-style.
newsitem.headline: Army has final say in democracy Turkish-style.

text.p: A broad cross-section of society, from elected officials to labour leaders and opinion makers, has cheered the army's latest intervention in domestic politics, reflecting a Turkish tradition at odds with textbook democracy.
In fact the generals are widely seen as saviors of Turkey's democratic order, stepping in to "adjust" the system as needed when events overwhelm fractious civilian leaders.
"Democracy in Turkey is based on the military, not on the republic," political commentator Mehmet Altan told Reuters.
Founded seven decades ago by military men from the ruins of the Ottoman Empire, the modern republic has never outgrown its martial provenance, say analysts.

The result is a society that relies on the army for its political and psychological well-being, ceding ultimate control to the soldiers despite such democratic trappings as free elections and a noisy press.
Three coups in the past 37 years each drew general approval from ordinary Turks, anxious to see the army make up for the perceived short-comings of elected leaders.

The military remains the most respected institution in the country, dwarfing parliament and the presidency in opinion polls. Officers wrote the current constitution and have resisted all attempts to introduce strict civilian controls.
The conscript army, the second largest in NATO, gobbles up a big chunk of national resources.
It directly rules nine mainly-Kurdish southeastern provinces but is almost never taken to task for alleged human rights abuses there that have tarnished Turkey's image in the West.
"The Turkish army does not protect the frontiers of Turkey, it protects the regime. It is protecting secularism," said Altan.
"It should be the people who should defend secularism."

This protective hand was clearly in evidence at the weekend, when the military-dominated National Security Council ordered Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan to crack down hard on religious fervour seen as threatening the secular order.
However, Erbakan's pleas to fellow politicians that the army was subverting democracy were widely ignored.
Party bosses, union chiefs and the mainsteam media all lectured the prime minister, modern Turkey's first Islamist leader, on the need to heed the demands of the army brass.

"The prime minister said it was a time for solidarity to protect democracy and that he expected cooperation from us," main opposition leader Mesut Yilmaz told reporters after meeting Erbakan on Wednesday.
"I told him I did not agree. I said it was up to him to clear up the problem," Yilmaz said.
Leftist leaders and the heads of three big trade unions, representing some six million members, all deserted the elected prime minister in face of the army's onslaught.

Nightly civil protests against the government have taken heart from the army demands, and a number of secularist intellectuals and commentators have all but urged the generals to depose the Islamist-led coalition.
"If you leave aside the 1980 coup, which was preceded by a civil war, the coups of 1960 and 1971 were both widely applauded," said analyst Ali Bayramoglu.
"It unfortunate to once again that this (intevention) is cheered by civic organisations, trade unions and artists, the press and academics.
"In Turkey there is not yet a democratic culture. Democracy is form, but we are more involved in the context," Bayramoglu said.
